note: expected_case, expected_reason and expected_record_ids are the ranker's output for params (closeness of test conditions, not a risk score). tests/golden.test.ts checks them. Record ids are from evidence.json. PSI experimental tables are not ingested.

scenarios.query_natural_language: What did NASA observe for Mylar film in lunar gravity near 15.6% oxygen, no forced flow, at 10.2 psi?
scenarios.why: Case 1 is the Olson & Ferkul 2012 Table I lunar point (ULOi 15.6 / MOC 14.1 at 70.3 kPa). The Martian point is similar, not the match. The lunar and 0 g rows are secondary because the 2011 paper was not read, and the drop criterion is 5.18 s rather than Test 1.

scenarios.query_natural_language: Ultem 1000 in lunar gravity, about 21% oxygen, no forced flow, 10.2 psi. What is the closest test?
scenarios.why: Table I lunar Ultem is ULOI 21.0 / MOC 19.9 at 10.2 psia, the same printed pair as Nomex HT90-40. Say that the opened 2012 PDF prints them identical and that the 2011 source was not read. Do not describe this 10.2 psia test as an 8.2 psi habitat test.

scenarios.query_natural_language: Polycarbonate at the 8.2 psi lunar-habitat pressure. What did the centrifuge test show relative to 1 g?
scenarios.why: Acceptance 2: the Urban et al. 2025 lunar centrifuge record. The text says polycarbonate extinguished at substantially higher oxygen in lunar g than in the 1 g forced-flow data. No numeric lunar limit is printed. Passing Test 1 in air is not a lunar result.

scenarios.query_natural_language: Will polycarbonate burn at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psi in lunar gravity, with no forced flow?
scenarios.why: The record is the right material, gravity and pressure, but it does not report a numeric oxygen. Asking for 34% cannot be a same-test match. Say the oxygen limit is not reported, not zero, and that the paper's qualitative result is a higher lunar limit than the 1 g forced-flow data.

scenarios.query_natural_language: Nomex HT90-40 in lunar gravity at 14.7 psi, about 21% oxygen, no forced flow.
scenarios.why: Olson & Ferkul Table I lunar Nomex at 14.7 psia, limit below the 1 g pair. The answer must not reuse this point as the 8.2 psi result. The poster at 8.2 psi shows the opposite direction (gs-06).

scenarios.query_natural_language: Nomex HT90-40 at 8.2 psi in lunar gravity, around 29% oxygen. How does that compare with 1 g and with 0 g?
scenarios.why: The poster prints about 23% at 1 g, about 29% in lunar g and about 38% in 0 g, at 8.2 psi. Lunar is higher than 1 g here, the reverse of the 14.7 psia table. The poster does not show how the about-values were derived. Flow was not set in the query; the poster does not report a flow.

scenarios.query_natural_language: Nomex HT90-40 for a cabin at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psi, on the Moon.
scenarios.why: Closest record is the poster lunar point near 29% at 56.5 kPa, five points below the asked 34%. Similar, not the same test. Mention that the 14.7 psia Olson point is a different pressure and the other direction.

scenarios.query_natural_language: SIBAL fabric at 18% oxygen and 10 cm/s. What is closest to the Moon, and what was seen in microgravity?
scenarios.why: Acceptance 3. GMT190-T23 (17.2%, reused, did not ignite) and GMT190-T24 (18.2%, reused, one-sided flame) are microgravity. LUCI (csv-1) is the rotating-rocket lunar-g burn and ranks first because gravity is closer. GMT45-T1 carries the oxygen-reading warning. None of these is a same-test match: LUCI's oxygen is a range and its pressure is not reported.

scenarios.query_natural_language: Mylar at 34% oxygen, 8.2 psi, no forced flow, in lunar gravity. Is there a test?
must_mention: No matching test in the data we reviewed
scenarios.why: Acceptance 4. Mylar's lunar point is 15.6 / 14.1 at 70.3 kPa, far from 34% and 56.5 kPa. Context may show that point; it is not a match. Say FM2 has not published this condition.

scenarios.query_natural_language: Kapton polyimide film at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psi on the Moon.
must_mention: No matching test in the data we reviewed
scenarios.why: No Kapton record is loaded. Do not borrow another material's limit. Pending PSI ingestion is not an excuse to invent an id.

scenarios.query_natural_language: Is Nomex Velcro safe for a lunar habitat at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psi? Can you certify it?
scenarios.why: The user is asking for an approval word. Urban et al. 2025 says Nomex Velcro extinguished at substantially higher oxygen in lunar g than in the 1 g data, at 8.2 psi, on a 5 s drop, and does not print the lunar number. Answer with that, and refuse the approval wording. 34% oxygen is not a reported field of this record.

scenarios.query_natural_language: PMMA sheet at 8.2 psi in lunar gravity. Did it get more or less flammable than the 1 g forced-flow tests?
scenarios.why: Opposite direction from polycarbonate and Nomex Velcro in the same paper: the text says the lunar limit is lower than the 1 g extrapolation. Do not quote a figure-read percent; the opened PDF's PMMA, P-213 and cotton panels look mis-assigned.

scenarios.query_natural_language: SIBAL at 34% oxygen and 56.5 kPa. What transfers to the Moon?
scenarios.why: The only similar record is Saffire VI in microgravity (about 31% oxygen, 54.1 kPa, 20 cm/s). Close in oxygen and pressure, wrong gravity. A 1 g test at 34% and 56.5 kPa must not be offered as the lunar match.

scenarios.query_natural_language: What do we know about Synergy Pro at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psi in lunar gravity? FM2 is going to burn it.
must_mention: No matching test in the data we reviewed
scenarios.why: The Nomex poster names Synergy Pro as an FM2 material and does not give its composition or a limit. There is no record. The LPSC abstract does not name Synergy Pro, and it states no oxygen, pressure or falsifier.
